Jurors weighing whether Massachusetts mother Lindsay Clancy was criminally responsible for killing her three young children told the court Tuesday they had been unable to reach a unanimous verdict, but the judge directed them to continue deliberating after more than three days of discussions.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
Jurors in the closely watched trial of Lindsay Clancy told a Massachusetts judge Tuesday that they had been unable to reach a unanimous decision on whether she was criminally responsible for killing her three young children, prompting the court to send them back for further deliberations.
The disclosure marked the first public indication that the jury had reached an impasse after more than three full days of deliberations.
Clancy, 36, sat facing forward as jurors entered the courtroom before turning her attention toward them while Judge William Sullivan addressed the panel.
“I know that this was a long trial, all right,” Sullivan said. “I know there were over 80 witnesses. There were over 300 exhibits. But because of that, I’m going to ask you to go back out.”
The jury began deliberating Thursday afternoon following more than four weeks of testimony centered on whether Clancy understood the wrongfulness of killing her children or was suffering from severe postpartum mental illness that left her without criminal responsibility.
Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility.
She does not dispute that she strangled her three children — Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months — but her attorneys argue that postpartum psychosis caused her to lose contact with reality.
Prosecutors contend that Clancy was depressed and suicidal but nevertheless understood what she was doing and made a conscious decision to kill the children before attempting to take her own life.
Jurors may convict Clancy of murder or manslaughter or acquit her if they conclude that her mental condition rendered her legally not responsible for the killings.
A murder conviction could result in a life prison sentence.
Even if Clancy is acquitted on the basis of lack of criminal responsibility, a judge could order her committed to a mental health facility if a subsequent evaluation determines that she remains a danger to the public.
Jury Previously Asked to Review Physical Evidence
Before Tuesday’s indication of a deadlock, the jury had offered few signs about the direction of its deliberations.
On Friday, jurors asked to examine a knife Clancy used to injure herself and bags containing empty prescription pill bottles recovered from the family home.
The physical evidence formed part of a much broader record that included testimony from more than 80 witnesses and more than 300 exhibits.
The case has generated intense public attention because of its focus on maternal mental illness following childbirth and sharply differing interpretations of Clancy’s condition before and during the killings.
Her defense maintains that she deeply loved her children but suffered a catastrophic psychiatric deterioration that ultimately caused her to lose her grasp on reality and on herself.
In the months before the deaths, Clancy sought help from multiple medical providers as her mental health worsened.
She also voluntarily admitted herself to a psychiatric hospital.
Less than three weeks after being discharged, prosecutors say, Clancy sent her husband away from their home on an errand and strangled all three children with exercise bands in the basement of their house south of Boston.
She then jumped from a second-floor window.
Clancy survived but remains paralyzed from the waist down.
Experts Offered Conflicting Views of Clancy’s Mental State
A central issue for jurors is the sharply conflicting expert testimony about what Clancy understood at the time of the killings.
A forensic psychologist called by prosecutors testified that he concluded Clancy killed her children because she intended to die by suicide and did not want to leave them behind.
A psychologist testifying for the defense reached a different conclusion, saying Clancy did not recognize the “wrongfulness” of killing her children because of her psychiatric condition.
Her mother and sister also testified during the trial, describing Clancy as increasingly anxious, paranoid and suicidal before the deaths.
Defense attorneys have identified postpartum psychosis as the condition responsible for her actions.
Postpartum psychosis is considerably rarer and more severe than postpartum depression.
Researchers estimate that it develops in approximately 1 to 2 women per 1,000 deliveries. Most women who experience the condition do not harm themselves or their children, but severe cases can involve delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thinking and an increased risk of self-harm or harm to others.
Prosecutors have argued that Clancy’s documented mental health struggles did not eliminate her ability to understand her actions.
They maintain that she planned the killings, waited until she was alone with the children and acted deliberately.
Patrick Clancy Testified for Two Days
Jurors also heard two days of testimony from Clancy’s former husband, Patrick Clancy.
His 911 call was played during the proceedings.
Patrick Clancy was still speaking with the emergency dispatcher when he discovered the bodies of his children, minutes after finding Lindsay Clancy seriously injured outside the house.
He has said publicly that he forgives his ex-wife and views what happened through the lens of severe illness rather than evil.
The trial was the first time Patrick Clancy had seen Lindsay Clancy since the killings.
Lindsay Clancy did not testify in her own defense.
She remained at the defense table throughout the proceedings and at times became visibly emotional, including when prosecutors showed jurors autopsy photographs of the children.
The jury must now return to deliberations after Sullivan declined to accept the initial impasse as final.
The panel’s eventual decision will turn on one of the central disputes presented throughout the trial: whether Clancy’s psychiatric condition deprived her of legal responsibility for killing Cora, Dawson and Callan, or whether she remained capable of understanding the nature and wrongfulness of her actions.

Lindsay Clancy trial jury DEADLOCKED in case of alleged child murderer
Jurors had spent more than 17 hours reviewing evidence
The panel of jurors deciding the fate of Lindsay Clancy has declared itself unable to reach agreement following three days of deliberations. Judge William Sullivan has directed the 12-member jury, comprising nine women and three men, to persist in their efforts to arrive at a unanimous decision.
The declaration of deadlock prompted audible gasps in the Massachusetts courtroom on Tuesday. The jury had spent more than 17 hours reviewing evidence before informing Judge Sullivan they could not agree on a verdict.
Clancy remained composed in her wheelchair beside her legal representative as the judge read out the jury's note. She was left paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window shortly after the killings.
The panel had heard weeks of testimony from dozens of witnesses before beginning their deliberations last week.
The 36-year-old former nurse faces three counts of first-degree murder over the deaths of her children in January 2023. Prosecutors contend she killed Cora, five, Dawson, three, and eight-month-old Callan through strangulation using fitness bands at the family's Massachusetts residence.
Her legal team does not contest that she ended the children's lives. However, they maintain she was experiencing postpartum psychosis at the time and lacked the capacity to differentiate between right and wrong.
The prosecution asserts her actions represented a calculated and intentional choice to kill her offspring. The central question before the jury concerns whether Clancy should face criminal punishment or be committed to a mental health facility.
She has entered a not-guilty plea to all murder charges.
The panel of jurors deciding the fate of Lindsay Clancy has declared itself unable to reach agreement
|REUTERS
A conviction on the most serious charge would result in a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment with no possibility of release. First-degree murder involves the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.
The jury is also weighing lesser charges that carry prison time but different standards. Second-degree murder would apply if the killings were committed with malice or extreme recklessness but without advance planning, whilst manslaughter would involve unintentionally causing death through wanton and reckless conduct.
Should the panel find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity, she would not walk free. Instead, she would be transferred to a psychiatric hospital where her condition would undergo periodic review.
Under this outcome, she could remain institutionalised for the remainder of her life.
LATEST DEVELOPMENTS
Should the impasse continue, Judge Sullivan may resort to what is termed a "dynamite charge", known formally in Massachusetts as Tuey-Rodriguez instructions. This measure would ask jurors to weigh the reasonableness of their own views and those of their fellow panel members whilst continuing to work towards agreement.
Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and expert in mental health law, told the BBC such instructions represent "typically a last-ditch effort" from a judge. She noted jury deadlocks occur in "complex and emotionally charged trials".
If unanimity proves impossible, a mistrial declaration would follow. Prosecutors would then face a choice: mount a second trial, abandon the case entirely, or attempt to reach a negotiated plea arrangement with Clancy.
It remains unclear whether the jury is divided on all charges or only certain counts.

The Lindsay Clancy trial hit a major impasse Tuesday after jurors informed the judge that they could not unanimously agree on any of the charges before them.
After roughly 18 hours of deliberations, the panel reported the deadlock. The judge, however, did not end deliberations and instead directed the jury to continue considering the case.
The Lindsay Clancy jury told the judge they are deadlocked on all counts
The Lindsay Clancy jurors must determine whether to find her guilty of murder, guilty of manslaughter or not guilty because of a lack of criminal responsibility. The latter option functions essentially as an insanity defense in the case.
Questions from the jury offered some indication of what evidence members were reviewing. During deliberations, jurors asked to examine the knife Clancy allegedly used to injure herself and the pill bottles connected to the case.
As per TMZ, the judge sent the panel back to continue deliberating, leaving the possibility of a Lindsay Clancy verdict unresolved.
Clancy has pleaded not guilty in connection with the January 2023 deaths of her three children, Cora, Dawson and Callan, at the family’s Massachusetts home. She has acknowledged killing the children, but her defense disputes her criminal responsibility at the time.
Defense attorney Kevin Reddington has argued that Clancy suffered from postpartum psychosis when the children died. Prosecutors have taken the opposite position and maintain that she remained criminally responsible for her actions.
The Lindsay Clancy murder case has also included testimony from her former husband, Patrick Clancy. He took the stand and described discovering his children at the family home. Jurors also heard his 911 call during the proceedings.
The reported Lindsay Clancy deadlocked jury does not yet mean the court will declare a mistrial. For now, the judge has instructed jurors to keep working toward a unanimous decision.
That leaves Clancy’s legal fate with the panel as deliberations continue across all counts.

Jurors in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy told a Massachusetts judge on Tuesday (September 1) that they were unable to reach a unanimous verdict over whether she should be convicted in the deaths of her three young children.
Judge William Sullivan, presiding over the trial in Plymouth, Massachusetts, instructed the jury to continue deliberating after receiving the note. The deliberations entered their fourth day Tuesday, following a trial that has lasted nearly six weeks.
“After many hours of deliberation, we are unable to come to a unanimous decision,” the jury said in its note, according to Sullivan.
The judge acknowledged the length of the trial but directed jurors to return to the deliberation room and continue considering the case while following the instructions he had given them.
A jury is considered hung when jurors cannot reach the unanimous decision required for a verdict after deliberating for an extended period.
However, Tuesday's note does not necessarily mean the jury is officially hung.
In this case, Sullivan has asked the jurors to continue deliberating. They could still reach a unanimous verdict and return to court with a decision.
If jurors ultimately remain deadlocked, the judge could declare a mistrial because of a hung jury. At that point, prosecutors could seek to retry the case with a new jury rather than accepting an acquittal.
A hung jury is different from a not-guilty verdict. If Clancy were acquitted, prosecutors generally could not retry her for the same offences because of protections against double jeopardy. A mistrial caused by a genuinely deadlocked jury, however, can allow a new trial.
Clancy, 36, is accused of killing her three children — 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan — at the family's home in Duxbury on January 24, 2023.
There is no dispute that the children died after being strangled with exercise bands in the basement of the home.
Clancy subsequently cut herself and jumped from a second-storey window in an apparent suicide attempt. She survived but was left paralysed.
Her defence attorney, Kevin Reddington, has argued that Clancy was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed the children. He has asked jurors to find her not guilty by reason of insanity.
Witnesses testified that Clancy later said she heard a man's voice telling her that she would lose her chance if she did not act. Reddington has argued that this was evidence of the psychotic episode he says she was experiencing at the time.
Prosecutors have focused on events immediately before the killings, including evidence that Clancy sent her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, out to collect a food order and visit a pharmacy.
Prosecutors highlighted evidence that she had mapped the time it would take him to return home.
When Patrick returned, he found Clancy injured in the backyard. He then went to the basement and discovered the children with exercise bands around their necks.
Clancy faces life in prison without parole if convicted of first-degree murder. If she is found not guilty by reason of insanity, she would instead be committed to a state psychiatric hospital for evaluation.
